page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The two configurations
lines: The ion has one electron more than the
steps.why: The stability argument is read directly off the two configurations, so both must be on the page before the reason is written.
common_mistakes: Writing the ion with one electron fewer instead of one more. Cl⁻ has GAINED an electron.
Writing 3p⁷ for the ion. The 3p subshell holds at most six electrons.
steps.memory_tip: The minus charge means one extra electron: 3p⁵ becomes 3p⁶.
steps.margin_note: Write both configurations one under the other so the 3p⁵ to 3p⁶ change is visible.

steps.label: The reason

lines.text: Cl⁻ has the stable inert gas configuration of argon

lines: Its outermost shell holds eight electrons
(a complete octet), so Cl⁻ is more stable
than the Cl atom, which has only seven.
steps.why: A complete octet in the outermost shell is the noble gas arrangement, which is the most stable one. The atom is one electron short of it; the ion has reached it.
common_mistakes: Saying the ion is stable because it is negative. The charge is not the reason; the completed octet is.
steps.memory_tip: Seven outer electrons in the atom, eight in the ion. Eight is the argon count.
steps.margin_note: Name argon (or write inert gas configuration). The bare word octet also earns it.

insider_note: Write both configurations — the examiner marks the pair, then the one sentence naming the inert gas configuration of the ion.
